vulnerability: Stale approval not cleared on transfer
reason: The `_transfer` function performs a transfer but never clears `getApproved[_tokenId]`. `_requireAuthorised` checks `msg.sender == getApproved[_tokenId]` alongside ownership. After a token is transferred to a new owner, any address previously approved by the old owner remains approved. That stale approved address can later call `transferFrom(newOwner, attacker, tokenId)`. The `_requireAuthorised` call will pass because `msg.sender == getApproved[_tokenId]` is true, and the subsequent `ownerOf(tokenId) == _from` check passes because `_from` is the current owner. The attacker can thus transfer the token to themselves, stealing it. This is a real-world exploitable NFT theft.

The require statement checks `data != IERC721TokenReceiver.onERC721Received.selector`, which is the opposite of the ERC721 standard. A compliant receiver contract returns the magic selector and should be accepted, but this code reverts in that case. Conversely, any contract returning an incorrect value (including a malicious contract) passes the check. This completely breaks safe transfer semantics: `safeTransferFrom` to correct receivers always reverts, while non-compliant or malicious contracts are accepted. An attacker can deploy a contract that returns an incorrect value but can still transfer the NFT out, tricking users into believing safe transfer succeeded while bypassing the intended receiver check. This can lead to NFT lockups or theft when users interact with malicious contracts that would otherwise fail a correct check.

The `transferFrom` function (and all transfer entry points) delegates to `_transfer`, which never emits the required ERC721 `Transfer` event. Off-chain indexers, wallets, and marketplaces rely on `Transfer` events to track ownership changes. An attacker can transfer an NFT to another address they control without any event being emitted. A marketplace that relies solely on event logs will still believe the attacker owns the NFT, allowing the attacker to list and sell it again. The buyer or marketplace may pay for an NFT that the attacker no longer owns, resulting in financial loss. This missing event enables double-spending and breaks ERC721 compliance, making it a severe integration vulnerability exploitable in real-world DeFi/NFT marketplaces.
